```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
ch_pums <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ifsUSH8veyhn8x8gUMo0MGu4VxYWpI9p", show_col_types = FALSE)
brfss <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=11rKXmplEk0dcvi7lzEQ0OUrXDrnvK4MR", show_col_types = FALSE)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
commuters_key <- ch_pums |> filter(travel_time_work > 0)
```

## Part 1: Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1: Load the Data

::: {.why}
We'll use `r fmt(nrow(ch_pums), 0)` American Community Survey records for people in the Chapel Hill area, from the Census Bureau's [Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS)](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/microdata/access.html). Each row is one person. `travel_time_work` is the one-way commute in minutes (0 for people who don't commute) and `public_health_ins` is 1 for people with public health insurance and 0 for everyone else. PUMS is really a weighted survey sample, but here we treat it as a simple random sample.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)

#Chapel Hill PUMS records
ch_pums <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ifsUSH8veyhn8x8gUMo0MGu4VxYWpI9p")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Histogram of one-way commute times for Chapel Hill commuters. Most commutes are between 5 and 30 minutes, with a long right tail of commutes over an hour."}
#keep only the people who commute
commuters <- ch_pums |> filter(travel_time_work > 0)

ggplot(commuters, aes(x = travel_time_work)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "One-way commute (minutes)", y = "Number of people")
```

### Step 2: Confidence Interval for a Mean by Hand

::: {.why}
The sample mean is the point estimate. The 95% confidence interval is $\bar{x} \pm t^* \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$. We use the t distribution for a mean because we estimate the population standard deviation from the sample.
:::

```{r}
x_bar <- mean(commuters$travel_time_work)
s <- sd(commuters$travel_time_work)
n <- nrow(commuters)

#critical value: 0.975 leaves 2.5% in each tail
t_star <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)

#margin of error, then the interval
margin <- t_star * s / sqrt(n)
c(x_bar - margin, x_bar + margin)
```

### Step 3: Confidence Interval for a Mean with `t.test()`

```{r}
t.test(commuters$travel_time_work, conf.level = 0.95)
```

The mean commute is `r fmt(mean(commuters_key$travel_time_work))` minutes, and the 95% confidence interval runs from `r fmt(t.test(commuters_key$travel_time_work)$conf.int[1])` to `r fmt(t.test(commuters_key$travel_time_work)$conf.int[2])` minutes. Change `conf.level` to 0.90 or 0.99 to see the interval get narrower or wider.

### Step 4: Confidence Interval for a Proportion

::: {.why}
For a proportion the interval is $\hat{p} \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$. `prop.test()` uses a slightly different formula (the Wilson interval with a continuity correction), so its answer differs a little from the hand calculation.
:::

```{r}
#by hand
p_hat <- mean(ch_pums$public_health_ins)
n_all <- nrow(ch_pums)
z_star <- qnorm(0.975)
p_margin <- z_star * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_all)
c(p_hat - p_margin, p_hat + p_margin)

#with prop.test (number of 1s, number of people)
prop.test(sum(ch_pums$public_health_ins), n_all, conf.level = 0.95)
```

## Part 2: Partner Practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners use answers from `r fmt(nrow(brfss), 0)` U.S. adults in the CDC's [Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS)](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/). `menthlth` is the number of days in the past 30 that the person's mental health was not good, `exerany2` is 1 if they exercised in the past 30 days and 0 if not, and `x.state` is the state's FIPS code (North Carolina is 37). Partner A estimates for North Carolina only and Partner B estimates for the whole sample. Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#BRFSS survey answers (both partners)
brfss <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=11rKXmplEk0dcvi7lzEQ0OUrXDrnvK4MR")
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: North Carolina

1. Keep only North Carolina with `filter(brfss, x.state == 37)`, and count your rows.
2. Find the mean of `menthlth` and its 95% confidence interval by hand. *(Step 2)*
3. Check your interval with `t.test()`. *(Step 3)*
4. Find the proportion who exercised and its 95% confidence interval with `prop.test()`. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your sample size, both estimates and both intervals to Part 3.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: Whole Sample

1. Use every row of `brfss`, and count your rows.
2. Find the mean of `menthlth` and its 95% confidence interval by hand. *(Step 2)*
3. Check your interval with `t.test()`. *(Step 3)*
4. Find the proportion who exercised and its 95% confidence interval with `prop.test()`. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your sample size, both estimates and both intervals to Part 3.
:::
::::

## Part 3: Together {#together}

1. Fill in the table.
2. Work out the width of each interval (upper minus lower). Whose intervals are wider, and by about how much?
3. Does Partner B's estimate fall inside Partner A's interval? What does that tell you about North Carolina compared with the whole sample?

| Sample | n | Mean poor mental health days (95% CI) | Proportion who exercised (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|
| North Carolina (Partner A) | | | |
| Whole sample (Partner B) | | | |

::: {.deliver}
Each pair turns in one index card before leaving. Write both of your names on it, copy the table, and add two or three sentences explaining why the North Carolina intervals are so much wider.
:::

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
nc_brfss <- brfss |> filter(x.state == 37)
ci_txt <- function(ci, d = 2) paste0(fmt(ci[1], d), " to ", fmt(ci[2], d))
a_m <- t.test(nc_brfss$menthlth); b_m <- t.test(brfss$menthlth)
a_p <- prop.test(sum(nc_brfss$exerany2), nrow(nc_brfss)); b_p <- prop.test(sum(brfss$exerany2), nrow(brfss))
w <- function(ci) ci[2] - ci[1]
```

| Sample | n | Mean poor mental health days (95% CI) | Proportion who exercised (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|
| North Carolina | `r nrow(nc_brfss)` | `r fmt(a_m$estimate)` (`r ci_txt(a_m$conf.int)`) | `r fmt(a_p$estimate, 3)` (`r ci_txt(a_p$conf.int, 3)`) |
| Whole sample | `r fmt(nrow(brfss), 0)` | `r fmt(b_m$estimate)` (`r ci_txt(b_m$conf.int)`) | `r fmt(b_p$estimate, 3)` (`r ci_txt(b_p$conf.int, 3)`) |

The hand calculation for the mean matches `t.test()`. The North Carolina intervals are about `r round(w(a_m$conf.int) / w(b_m$conf.int))` times wider for the mean and `r round(w(a_p$conf.int) / w(b_p$conf.int))` times wider for the proportion. The whole-sample estimates fall inside the North Carolina intervals, so these data give no evidence that North Carolina differs from the whole sample.

A good card says something like this. The margin of error shrinks with the square root of n. Partner A had only `r nrow(nc_brfss)` people and Partner B had `r fmt(nrow(brfss), 0)`, about `r round(nrow(brfss) / nrow(nc_brfss))` times as many, so Partner B's intervals are roughly √`r round(nrow(brfss) / nrow(nc_brfss))`, or about `r round(sqrt(nrow(brfss) / nrow(nc_brfss)))`, times narrower. A small sample can still give a sensible estimate, but we are much less sure where the true value is.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
brfss <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=11rKXmplEk0dcvi7lzEQ0OUrXDrnvK4MR")

#### Partner A: North Carolina ####
nc_brfss <- brfss |> filter(x.state == 37)
nrow(nc_brfss)

x_bar <- mean(nc_brfss$menthlth)
s <- sd(nc_brfss$menthlth)
n <- nrow(nc_brfss)
margin <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * s / sqrt(n)
c(x_bar - margin, x_bar + margin)

t.test(nc_brfss$menthlth, conf.level = 0.95)
prop.test(sum(nc_brfss$exerany2), nrow(nc_brfss), conf.level = 0.95)

#### Partner B: whole sample ####
nrow(brfss)

x_bar <- mean(brfss$menthlth)
s <- sd(brfss$menthlth)
n <- nrow(brfss)
margin <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * s / sqrt(n)
c(x_bar - margin, x_bar + margin)

t.test(brfss$menthlth, conf.level = 0.95)
prop.test(sum(brfss$exerany2), nrow(brfss), conf.level = 0.95)
```
